(A.) -A2- [Hence,] nasarahu (tropical:) He blamed him; found fault with him; spoke evil of him behind his back, or in his absence, saying of him what would grieve him if he heard it. (A.)

10 He (the bagaAv [or ignoble bird, or most ignoble of birds,] S, M) became a nasor [or vulture ]: (M:) or became like the nasor (S, K) in strength. (K.) Hence the proverb, A_in~a AlbagaAva biA^aroDinaA yasotanosiru [ Verily the most ignoble bird, or most ignoble birds, in our land becomes like the vulture, or become like vultures ]: (S, M:) meaning, the weak among us becomes strong. (S.) See also art. bgv .

(S, M, Msb, K, &c.) and sometimes ↓ [agreeably with the modern general pronunciation] and ↓ , (Sheykh-el-Islám Zekereeyà, in his Comm. on the Expos. of Bd,) but this is very strange, (MF,) [The vulture; app. any vulture, whatever be its species or variety, known to the Arabs, except the raxam , or aquiline vulture; and said to be applied by some of the Arabs to the eagle; (see also nusaAriy~apN ;) agreeing with the Hebrew , which is plainly applied to the former bird in Micah, i. 16, and probably in other instances;] a certain bird, (S, M, A, Msb, K,) well known; (A, Msb;) so called because it plucks ( yanosuiru ) a thing, and swallows it, (A, and so in some copies of the K,) or, and pulls it out (so in some copies of the K,) or, and chases and captures it; (so in some copies of the K; the

22 and 23: (S, M:) or a certain good man, who lived between Adam and Noah, and of whom, after his death, was made an image, which, after a long time, became an object of worship; like wad~N and suwaAEN and yaguwvu , and yaEuwqu , mentioned therewith in the Kur, ubi supra. (Bd.) -A3-

Also, nasorN [The frog, or frush, of the hoof of a horse or ass or mule; thus called in the present day;] a portion of tough flesh, [or rather a horny substance, ] in the bTon [or sole ] of the solid hoof, as though it were a datestone, [which it resembles in substance,] or a pebble: (S:) or the flesh of the solid hoof, which the poets liken to date-stones: (T:) or a portion of flesh, (K,) or of hard flesh, (M,) in the baATin [or sole, or inner part, ] of the solid hoof, (M, K, TA,) as though it were a pebble, or a date-stone, (TA:) or what rises in the bATn of the hoof of the horse, from, or of, the upper part thereof: (M, K:) or the bATn itself of the solid hoof: (M:) pl. nusuwrN , (M, K,) which Aboo-Sa'eed explains as signifying the prominences in the baTon [or sole ] of the solid hoof,

The eagle; syn. EuqaAbN : (IAar, K:) likened to the nasor . (IAar, TA.) [Hence it appears that, accord. to IAar, the nasor is not the eagle.]

(also written with S , S, Msb,) A certain disease that happens in the inner angles of the eyes, (S, Msb, K,) with an incessant defluxion therefrom: (S, TA:) and sometimes it happens also in the part around the anus: and in the gum: (S, Msb:) or it signifies also a certain disease in the part around the anus: and a certain disease in the gum: (K:) and is an arabicized word [from the Persian]: (S, Msb:) nawaASiyr , pl. of naASuwrN , accord. to certain of the physicians, is a term applied to deep ulcers in the anus, at the extremity of the gut. (S, Msb.) -A2- [Hence,] ↓ both words also signify (assumed tropical:) A portion of an army that goes before the main army: (S, K:) [likened to the beak of a bird of prey; as the side bodies are likened to the wings:] and a troop of horse or horsemen in number from thirty to forty: or from forty to fifty: or from forty to sixty: (M, K:) or from a hundred to two hundred: (M, Msb, K:) or a troop of horse or horsemen: (El-Farábee, Msb:) or an army that does not pass by anything without snatching it away. (Msb.)

; or of beginning to do so: and it (water) made a sound in pouring forth. (TA.) And Ald~iroEu ↓ The coat of mail made a sound, (K,) or clinking. (Fr.) ― -b2-

(Sh, from certain of the Kilábees.) -A2- Also na$~a , aor. , inf. n. na$iy$N (S, K) and na$~N , (TA,) said of a pool of water left by a torrent, Its water began to sink into the earth: (S, K:) or its water dried up, and sank into the earth. senses.text: 1 , (S, K, &c.,) aor. , (S, Msb. &c.,) inf. n. na$odN (L, Msb, K) and ni$odapN and ni$odaAnN , (S, M, L, K,) or these two are simple substs., (Msb,) He raised his voice in seeking for, or after, a stray-beast, or beast that had been lost; he called out and inquired respecting it; he cried it: (L:) or he sought for, or after, it: (Lh, A'Obeyd, S, M, L, Msb, K:) and [in like manner] ↓ he asked, or desired, to be directed to it. (M, L, K.) ― -b2-

Also, He made known, or gave information of, a stray-beast, or beast that had been lost; (Lh, A'Obeyd, M, L, Msb K;) and so ↓ : (Lh, S, M, IKtt, L, Msb, K:) thus the latter verb [as well as the former] bears two contr. significations. (M, K.) See also naA$idN . ― -b3- na$ada (assumed tropical:) He sought, sought for or after, or desired, a thing. (L.) ― -b4- na$adahu (assumed tropical:) He asked, begged, or besought, him. (L.) ― -b5- nu$ida (assumed tropical:) He was asked, begged, or besought. (S, L.) See 6: and

(TA.) (L.) ― -b6- nakada HaAjatahu , aor. ; (K;) or nakadahu HaAjatahu , (L,) He withheld from him, or refused him, his want. The young one of a raven, or crow: syn faroxu guraAbK : or a raven, or crow, [absolutely]: syn. EuraAbN . In a prayer of David occur the words yaA raAziq Aln~aE~aAbi fiY Eu$~ihi [ O Sustainer of the young raven (or young crow ) in his nest! ]. It is said that the young raven (or young crow), when it comes forth from its egg, is white, like a lump of fat, and that the old bird, on seeing it, dislikes and abandons it; that thereupon God sends to it gnats, which light upon it on account of its foul greasy smell, and that it lives upon them until it is fledged and becomes black, when its parents return to it. (L.)

A^anowaA='N and nuwA=nN , (S, K,) A star, or an asterism, verging to setting: or the setting of the star, or asterism, in the west, aurorally, i. e., at dawn of morning, and the rising of another, opposite to it, at the same time, in the east: (K:) or the setting of one of the stars, or asterisms, which compose the Mansions [ of the Moon (see manaAzilu Alqamari )], in the west, aurorally, i. e., at dawn of morining, and the rising of its raqiyb , which is another star, or asterism, opposite to it, at the same time, in the east, each night for a period of thirteen days: thus does each star, or asterism, of those Mansions, [one after another,] to the end of the year, except Aljabohap , the period of which is fourteen days: (S:) [or it signifies the auroral rising, and sometimes the aur

; or, accord. to As, to that which was rising in its ascendency [ aurorally ]; and used to say, muTironaA binawo'i ka*aA [ We have been given rain by such a nw' ]; (S;) or they attributed heat [and cold] to the rising or the star or asterism, and rain [and wind], to its nawo' [meaning its setting ]. (AHn, Har, p.

216.) This the Muslim is forbidden to say, unless he mean thereby, “ We have been given rain at the period of such a nw' ; ” God having made it usual for rain to come at [certain of] the periods called AnwA' . Again, A'Obeyd says, The AnwA' are twenty-eight stars, or asterisms; sing. nw' : the rising of any one of them in the east [ aurorally ] is called nw' ; and the star, or asterism, itself is hence thus called: but sometimes nw' signifies the setting.

Also, in the L it is said, that each of the abovementioned stars, or asterisms, is called thus because, when that in the west sets, the opposite one rises; and this rising is called Aln~w' ; but some make nw' to signify the setting; as if it bore contr. senses. (TA.) [El-Kazweenee mentions certain physical occurrences on the occasions of the AnwA' of the Mansions of the Moon; and in each of these cases, except three, the nw' is the rising, not the setting. Hence, again, it appears most probable, that the rising, not the setting, was generally called nw' .] ― -b3- [In many instances,] AlA^anowaA='u signifies The Mansions of the Moon [themselves]; and nawo'N , any one of those Mansions: and they are also called nujuwmu AlmaTari [ the stars, or asterisms, of rain ]. (Mgh, in art. xTA^ .) IAar says that the term nw' was not applied except in the case of a star, or asterism, accompanied by rain: (TA:) [see exs. under xaT~a and xaT~aA^a : but most authors, it seems, apply this term without such restriction: it is sometimes given to certain stars or asterisms, which do not belong to the Mansions of the Moon; as will be seen below: and it is applied, with the article, especially to Alv~uray~aA ]. ― -b4- Accord. to AZ, as cited by AM, the first rain
